coverage_note: Read the full relay layer (relay_provider, relay_session, relay_socket, relay_client, relay_validation, media_upload, media_auth, media_image, nostr_models, signed_event_relay, app_lifecycle_provider, relay.dart barrel), both deeplink files, both invite files, and the pairing feature (pairing_provider, pairing_crypto, pairing_socket, pairing_page, pairing_qr_scanner + its part files). Traced the relay URL end to end: deep_link.parseInviteDeepLink -> InviteDeepLink.relayUrl ("wss://host") -> InviteJoinNotifier.confirmJoin -> Community.create(relayUrl:) -> RelayConfigNotifier.build -> RelayConfig.baseUrl -> {RelayConfig.wsUrl -> RelaySocket, RelaySessionNotifier.queryRelay, MediaUploadService._buildUploadRequest, MediaGetAuthService, RelayClient.mediaUploadUrl}; and the pairing path parseNostrpairUri/_parseLegacyInput -> _validateRelayUrl -> Community.create(relayUrl: "https://host"). Did NOT read (not present in this subset): shared/community/community_provider.dart (Community.create / nameFromUrl / communityListProvider), shared/auth/auth.dart, shared/crypto/{ecdh,nip44,hkdf}.dart, and the `nostr` package itself — so I could not confirm whether Community.create re-normalizes relayUrl (every helper in invite_join_provider switches on 'wss'/'ws', and pairing's validator only accepts http/https, which is strong evidence the two paths persist different schemes). Skimmed only: animated_image_sanitizer.dart, mp4_fast_start.dart, nostr_filters.dart, and the pure-UI part files (onboarding_background, pairing_welcome_view, dynamic_island_portal, scanner_camera).

findings.claim: RelayConfig.wsUrl silently downgrades TLS for every community joined by invite link. The scheme test only recognises 'https', but the invite path persists the relay URL with the websocket scheme ('wss://host'), so 'wss' falls into the else branch and the socket is opened as plaintext 'ws://'. The wss-only validation performed at parse time (relay_validation.validateInviteRelayUri throws 'Relay URL must use WSS') therefore does not survive to the connection actually made.
findings.failure_scenario: User opens https://relay.example/invite/abc123. parseInviteDeepLink builds relayUrl = 'wss://relay.example' (deep_link.dart:197-213) and validateInviteRelayUri accepts it because the scheme is wss. confirmJoin stores that exact string as Community.relayUrl (invite_join_provider.dart:157-162), and RelayConfigNotifier.build sets baseUrl = 'wss://relay.example'. On connect, wsUrl computes uri.scheme=='wss' != 'https' -> scheme='ws' -> 'ws://relay.example'. RelaySocket.connect opens an unencrypted WebSocket on port 80 and immediately sends the NIP-42 kind:22242 AUTH event signed with the member's nsec (relay_socket.dart:203-217), plus every subsequent message and subscription, in cleartext. Any on-path attacker (café Wi-Fi, ISP, hostile CGNAT) reads the whole community feed, replays the AUTH event, and — because inbound events are never signature-checked (see relay_session.dart:449) — injects arbitrary forged messages. The invite claim itself went over HTTPS (_claimUrlFromRelay maps wss->https), so nothing warns the user.

findings.claim: The pairing path validates the relay URL with a hand-rolled private-address check that is far weaker than the hardened shared validator (relay_validation.dart) used by the invite path — the same stored field, two different validators. _isPrivateHost only understands 4-part dotted-decimal and only blocks 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 and 169.254/16, and the localhost check is three exact strings.
findings.failure_scenario: A user scans a hostile QR (or a compromised/malicious 'source' device sends a pairing payload) whose relayUrl is 'https://127.0.0.2/', 'https://127.1/', 'https://2130706433/', 'https://[0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1]/', 'https://0.0.0.0/', 'https://100.64.3.9/' (CGNAT) or 'https://foo.localhost/'. None of these match host=='localhost'|'127.0.0.1'|'::1', and _isPrivateHost returns false for all of them ('127.1' and '2130706433' are not 4 parts; '127.0.0.2' has a=127 which is not in the list; the IPv6 form splits on '.' into 1 part; 100.64/10 is absent). The app then opens a WebSocket to that address with the supplied nsec and, on success, stores it as the active community, so the device is pointed at loopback/link-local/CGNAT services the user cannot see. The invite path routed through validateInviteRelayUri would have rejected every one of these (relay_validation.dart:38-62 rejects non-canonical IPv4 literals, all of 127/8, 100.64/10, 0/8, and non-global IPv6).

findings.claim: The SAS-verified NIP-AB pairing protocol can be skipped entirely by prefix choice: any scanned string that does not start with 'nostrpair://' is routed to the legacy base64 path, which imports a relay URL AND an nsec from the QR with no ECDH, no SAS code, no transcript hash, and no user confirmation screen.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker prints/AirDrops/embeds a QR containing 'buzz://<base64 of {"relayUrl":"https://evil.example","pubkey":"...","nsec":"<attacker-known key>"}>'. pair() sees no 'nostrpair://' prefix and calls _pairLegacy, which decodes the payload, connects once to validate, and calls authenticateWithCommunity — the SAS screen (_SasVerificationView, the only thing that asks 'Does your desktop app show this code?') never appears. The victim is now signed in to an attacker-controlled relay under an identity whose private key the attacker holds: the attacker can read everything the victim posts, sign messages as the victim, and — because the same QR scanner is offered from the invite success sheet's 'Back it up now' button (invite_join_sheet.dart:171-182) — the victim believes they are backing up their real identity.

findings.claim: MediaGetAuthService._isRelayMediaUrl matches on authority only and explicitly accepts 'http' as well as 'https', so a signed Blossom kind:24242 't=get' credential is attached to plaintext HTTP media fetches. extractServerAuthority also strips ':80'/':443' regardless of scheme, so 'http://relay.example:80/media/x' and 'wss://relay.example' normalise to the identical authority.
findings.failure_scenario: Any relay event (message imeta tag, profile picture, custom emoji) that contains 'http://relay.example/media/evil.jpg' passes isRelayMediaUrl, so MediaImageProvider._loadAsync sends the memoized 'Authorization: Nostr <base64 kind:24242 event>' header over unencrypted HTTP (media_image.dart:95). That auth event carries only ['t','get'], ['expiration'] and ['server'] tags — it is not bound to a URL or body hash (media_auth.dart:109-114) — so a passive network observer captures a bearer token valid for the full 600-second lifetime and can read any media blob on the relay as that user. On an invite-joined community the relay base URL is already 'wss://…' (finding 1), so the authority comparison succeeds while nothing in this class ever checks that the fetch is encrypted.

findings.claim: MediaUploadService rebuilds the upload URL by resolving a path against the stored baseUrl, assuming baseUrl is HTTP-schemed. For invite-joined communities baseUrl is 'wss://host', so the request target becomes 'wss://host/upload', which package:http/dart:io cannot issue — a consumer that disagrees with RelayConfig.wsUrl about what the same stored string means.
findings.failure_scenario: A member who joined via an invite link picks a photo; _buildUploadRequest produces Uri 'wss://relay.example/upload' and _http.send throws ArgumentError('Unsupported scheme wss in …') before any network I/O. Both the primary and the /media/upload legacy retry fail the same way, so media upload is permanently broken for every invite-joined community while working for pairing-joined ones (which store 'https://…'). RelayClient.mediaUploadUrl (relay_client.dart:21-24) has the identical defect.

findings.claim: queryRelay resolves the relay's HTTP bridge endpoint against config.baseUrl with no scheme mapping, so it inherits whatever scheme the onboarding path persisted — 'https://host/query' for pairing, but 'wss://host/query' for invites. The NIP-98 header is also signed over that malformed URL.
findings.failure_scenario: On an invite-joined community every one-shot query throws at client.post(Uri.parse('wss://relay.example/query')) — the http client rejects the wss scheme — so all HTTP-bridge queries fail for exactly the users onboarded by invite link. Note the invite provider itself knows the mapping is required and does it locally (_claimUrlFromRelay switches wss->https, invite_join_provider.dart:242-255); relay_session does not, which is the concrete divergence between two consumers of the same stored value.

findings.claim: Inbound relay events are deserialized with NostrEvent.fromJson, which copies id/pubkey/sig verbatim and performs no id recomputation and no Schnorr signature check (nostr_models.dart:113-125). Nothing else in the session layer verifies them, so authorship of every displayed message rests entirely on the transport.
findings.failure_scenario: Anyone who can write frames on the socket — a malicious or compromised relay, or an on-path attacker on the plaintext ws:// connection created by finding 1 — sends ['EVENT','l-1',{'id':'…','pubkey':'<admin pubkey>','kind':9,'content':'send me your seed','sig':'00…'}]. _handleEvent constructs the NostrEvent and delivers it to the live subscription callback; the UI renders it as an authentic message from the admin. The pairing code path shows the intended contrast — it explicitly verifies signatures before acting (pairing_provider.dart:334-341) — while the main event path does not.

findings.claim: _validateCredentials duplicates the same defective scheme mapping as RelayConfig.wsUrl ('https' -> wss, everything else -> ws), so the credential-validation handshake silently drops to plaintext for any relayUrl that is not literally https-schemed.
findings.failure_scenario: In a debug build (or if _validateRelayUrl is ever relaxed, or if this helper is reused for an invite-shaped 'wss://' URL as _processPayload's sibling paths already are), uri.scheme is 'http' or 'wss' and the else branch yields 'ws://…'. The user's real nsec is then used to sign a NIP-42 AUTH event and sent over an unencrypted socket during what the code calls 'validation'. Two copies of the same wrong mapping mean fixing relay_provider.dart alone does not fix the app.

findings.claim: parseNostrpairUri accepts plaintext 'ws://' relays and applies no host validation at all — no TLS requirement, no private/loopback address filtering — unlike validateInviteRelayUri which is applied to every invite relay.
findings.failure_scenario: A hostile QR code carries 'nostrpair://<64 hex>?secret=<64 hex>&relay=ws://192.168.0.5:7777'. _pairNipAb passes qr.relays.first straight to PairingSocket with no further checks (pairing_provider.dart:178, 198-205), so the device opens an unencrypted WebSocket to an arbitrary attacker-chosen host on the local network. The pairing payload itself is NIP-44 encrypted and SAS-bound, so key material is not directly exposed, but the ephemeral pubkey, the source pubkey p-tag, timing metadata, and the NIP-42 AUTH event are sent in the clear, and the scanner becomes a probe for internal hosts.

findings.claim: Relay frames are type-cast without checking: data[0] is cast to String in both socket layers, and relay_session casts data[1]/data[2]/data[3] to String/Map/bool inside stream callbacks that have no try-catch around the dispatch.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious relay (or on-path attacker on the downgraded ws:// link) sends '[1]' or '["EVENT","l-1","not-an-object"]' or '["OK","id","yes"]'. The cast raises a TypeError inside the WebSocket stream listener rather than being swallowed like malformed JSON is on the line above, producing an uncaught async error; _handleOk's 'data[2] as bool' and _handleEvent's 'data[2] as Map<String, dynamic>' (relay_session.dart:447) fail the same way. A single crafted frame is enough to disrupt the session, and the surrounding code's own comments assume malformed input is merely ignored.
